title: Jeff Garlin Contemplates Suicide After Turbulent ‘Goldbergs’ Exit, Hollywood Reporter Reveals
body:
The beloved “Barney” of ABC’s long‑running sitcom The Goldbergs has opened up about a harrowing personal crisis that followed his abrupt departure from the series. Jeff Garlin, who played the boisterous, often‑drunk father Murray Goldberg, revealed that after an internal HR investigation into multiple complaints about his on‑set conduct, he fell into a deep depressive state and briefly entertained thoughts of suicide. In a candid interview, Garlin disclosed that he reached out to longtime co‑star and onscreen wife, Susie Essman—best known for her role on “Curb Your Enthusiasm”—to confide his plans and seek a lifeline.

Garlin’s exit from The Goldbergs came after more than a decade of portraying the chaotic patriarch whose antics anchored the show’s nostalgic 1980s setting. The investigation, launched by ABC Studios in early 2024, stemmed from a series of allegations by crew members and fellow actors describing Garlin’s behavior as “unprofessional” and “intimidating.” While the network has not released the full findings, it confirmed that the investigation concluded with a mutual agreement for Garlin to leave the series. The actor’s sudden disappearance from the final episodes of season ten left fans bewildered, sparking speculation about the underlying reasons.

In the interview, Garlin described the period after his departure as a “dark tunnel” that threatened to consume him. “I was in a place where I didn’t see any way out,” he said, explaining that the loss of his daily routine, the camaraderie of the cast, and the identity tied to his character amplified his sense of isolation. He confessed that he drafted a note to his mother and considered ending his life, but a phone call from Essman altered the course. “She listened without judgment, reminded me that I’m more than a role, and helped me see there’s still a future worth fighting for,” Garlin recounted.

Industry insiders note that Garlin’s struggle underscores a broader conversation about mental health in Hollywood, particularly for actors whose public personas mask private turmoil. The entertainment world has seen an uptick in high‑profile disclosures of depression, anxiety, and substance abuse, prompting studios to bolster employee assistance programs and destigmatize seeking help. However, critics argue that the same environments that foster creative brilliance can also exacerbate stress, especially when allegations of misconduct lead to swift professional fallout. Garlin’s case illustrates how the intersection of workplace investigations and personal accountability can have unintended psychological repercussions.

The fallout from Garlin’s departure also reverberates within The Goldbergs’ production team. Showrunner Adam F. Goldberg issued a brief statement expressing gratitude for Garlin’s contributions while emphasizing the series’ commitment to a respectful workplace. The show has since introduced a new character to fill the paternal void, and producers say they are consulting mental‑health professionals to support the remaining cast and crew. Fans have responded with a mixture of empathy and concern, flooding social media with messages of support for Garlin and calls for more compassionate handling of similar situations in the industry.

Looking ahead, Garlin indicated that he is seeking professional therapy and has taken a hiatus from acting to focus on his recovery. He expressed a tentative optimism about returning to the screen, emphasizing that any future projects will be chosen with an eye toward healthier environments. His openness may serve as a catalyst for broader change, encouraging studios to adopt more robust mental‑health resources and to approach investigations with a balanced perspective that safeguards both workplace safety and individual well‑being. As the conversation around celebrity mental health evolves, Garlin’s story stands as a stark reminder that behind the laughter of sitcoms lie real people navigating very real challenges.
